hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick

My thoughts on stevia, monk fruit, and allulose. These are three sugar alternatives I get asked about a lot.

Stevia - Some human research suggests modest benefits for blood glucose regulation and possibly blood pressure, although findings are mixed.

Monk fruit - One of my preferred alternatives to sugar. It has little effect on blood glucose, but long-term human safety data are limited. One caution: Many monk fruit products contain mostly erythritol, which I personally try to avoid because of emerging research on platelet activation.

Allulose - Small human studies suggest it may actually reduce post-meal glucose and insulin spikes. Promising, but we need more long-term research.

None of these were included in the recent study linking sugar substitutes to cognitive decline.

My personal approach? I generally favor stevia or pure monk fruit when I need a little sweetness, and I'm cautiously optimistic about allulose. But I try to minimize added sweeteners overall.
hits.draft_en:

Stevia: some research hints at modest help with blood sugar and maybe blood pressure, but it's mixed.
Monk fruit: one of her picks, little effect on blood sugar. Catch: lots of monk fruit products are mostly erythritol, which she avoids.
Allulose: small studies suggest it may cut post-meal sugar and insulin spikes. Promising, needs more research.

Her rule: stevia or pure monk fruit when she wants a bit of sweet, and keep added sweeteners down overall. Read the label on the packet.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩

Your knee didn’t just decide to hurt one day. It was slowly cooked.

Every time you eat white bread, pasta, rice, or anything made from refined flour, your blood sugar jumps hard and fast. That glucose doesn’t just sit there. It sticks to proteins. Permanently. The process is called glycation, and the end product is something called an AGE. Advanced glycation end-product. It sounds technical. It means your collagen gets caramelized while it’s still inside you.

Cartilage is mostly collagen. And cartilage doesn’t turn over. The same stuff you had at twenty is the same stuff you’re standing on at fifty. Once it’s glycated, it gets stiff and brittle. It loses the spring that lets it absorb impact. Then it starts to break down. Inflammation follows. The joint swells. The pain starts.

This isn’t theory. Higher dietary glycemic load is linked to worse knee osteoarthritis symptoms and higher levels of inflammatory markers. In animal and cell studies, the same high-sugar environment drives synovial inflammation and accelerates cartilage breakdown. Low-carbohydrate trials, even small ones, have repeatedly shown reductions in pain and stiffness in people with knee osteoarthritis, often outperforming low-fat diets even when weight loss is similar.

The modern Western diet is built on these refined carbs. They drive the insulin spikes, the visceral fat, the low-grade inflammation, and the steady accumulation of AGEs in tissues that can’t repair themselves. Your joints are among the most vulnerable.
Nobody warns you that the sandwich is aging your knees faster than your birthdays. They just tell you to take the pill and keep eating the bread.

The cartilage doesn’t get a vote. It just gets glycated.

Just finished a fascinating interview with a newly diagnosed type 1 diabetic who went carnivore

He had always eaten a clean healthy diet of lean meats organic fruits and vegetables, rice and was regularly in the gym and weighed around 200lbs but always had gut issues 

At age 37 he started losing weight despite eating more and more food. Started eating ice cream and other junk food just to try and keep his weight on. Despite that he became skin and bones dropping to 150 lbs and was constantly thirsty and urinating. 

Went to doctor was found to have a HBA1C above 14 and was diagnosed as a type 1 diabetic when his C-peptide was essentially zero and his diabetes autoantibodies were all extremely high. 

Was started on insulin and told to eat a mostly plant based diet. 

He followed directions to the tee and was having blood glucose swings from profound hypoglycemia up to over 400mg/dl

Eventually he decided to go carnivore to help with his gut issues against the advice of his care team. 

He was not expecting to get off insulin

Soon after that he noticed he was requiring less and less insulin

1 month ago, a full year after his diagnosis, he stopped taking his insulin as his blood glucose kept going too low.  He now has a blood glucose range of about 70-130 with an average of mid 90s with zero insulin and a carnivore diet. 

This is likely a prolongation of his honeymoon period. But, nonetheless, very interesting to see. We know that type 1 diabetics that utilize a lot of insulin often are at increased risk of cancer so it’s better if they can keep the requirements relatively low. 

Next week he is repeating labs to check his C-peptide, antibodies and A1C. 

Will be interesting to see how things go over next few months/years

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Where does red meat fit in a healthy diet?

Dr. Dariush Mozaffarian offers a hierarchy for the animal foods: fermented dairy at the top (yogurt, then cheese), unprocessed red meat below it, and processed meat at the bottom.

Processed meat has a consistent link with colorectal cancer. I’ve discussed one plausible mechanism: nitrites used in curing can form nitrosamines that damage DNA.

Unprocessed red meat is more nuanced.

When it's analyzed separately from processed meat, the association with disease is weaker and less consistent. Some long-term observational studies still link higher intake with type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer, and heme iron or other components may contribute. But short, randomized trials have generally shown little or inconsistent change in glucose control and blood markers of inflammation.

I think the useful questions are how often you eat meat, how it’s processed, and what the rest of your diet looks like. Red meat can provide valuable nutrients, including high-quality protein, iron, zinc, and vitamin B12. 

When I consume it a few times per week, I tend to emphasize high-quality sources like grass-fed beef, while also prioritizing seafood, eggs, and a wide variety of plant foods.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Many people believe fat cells grow on calories alone, but that idea leaves out a key requirement. Fat cell growth requires both a signal and a substrate. Calories are the substrate, the raw material that gets stored. Insulin is the signal that tells fat cells to take that material in and grow. Without the signal, the substrate becomes meaningless.

Some of the clearest human evidence comes from people who inject insulin into the same small patch of skin for years. All of their fat tissue is exposed to the same calories in the blood, but only the fat at the injection site gets a concentrated dose of insulin, and that's the fat that grows. Among people with type 1 diabetes, 62% have a lump of extra fat at an injection site, called lipohypertrophy. The strongest predictors are injecting into a small area and failing to rotate sites.

The size these lumps can reach is remarkable. One case study from Kyoto described a woman with type 2 diabetes, treated with insulin for 16 years, who developed two soft masses of about 10 cm at her lower abdominal injection sites. The tissue removed weighed 405 grams and consisted entirely of fat. Under the microscope, the fat cells bathed in high insulin measured 100 to 200 micrometers across compared with 70 to 90 in the surrounding tissue, which made them roughly twice the diameter and about six times larger in volume. Small new fat cells sat among the enlarged ones, which pointed to insulin both enlarging fat cells and recruiting new ones right where it was delivered. Again, is the signal. 

The man in the photo is from another case study. He had lived with type 1 diabetes for 40 years and had two lumps more than 10 cm across where he repeatedly injected. 

The same rule holds across the whole body. In untreated type 1 diabetes, people waste away even while eating plenty, because the substrate is there but the signal is missing. Once insulin starts, children with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes gain an average of 9% of their body weight within two weeks and nearly 13% within about six weeks. Adults with type 1 diabetes who move to intensive insulin therapy without eating any more gain 2.4 kg of body fat in two months.

Taken together, it's clear that calories alone aren't enough to build fat. Fat cell growth requires the substrate and the signal together, and insulin is that signal.

Great question! Here's the very interesting answer...
Let's follow the glyphosate through the cow.

It starts in the rumen, which is basically a giant fermentation vat full of microbes. When German researchers fed dairy cows the glyphosate levels found in real feed, part of it seemed to disappear right there in the rumen, likely broken down by those microbes before it ever reached the intestines.

Insulin resistance in muscle can push the carbohydrate from a meal into the liver, where it's turned into fat, even in young, lean people.

Muscle is the main place the body stores carbohydrate after a meal, in the form of glycogen. When muscle responds well to insulin, much of the glucose from a carbohydrate-rich meal ends up there.

Young, lean adults with insulin-resistant muscle store far less glycogen in muscle after two high-carbohydrate meals than equally lean, equally active peers who are insulin sensitive. That glucose doesn't disappear. The liver handles more of it, and its production of new fat from carbohydrate more than doubles, along with its production of triglycerides.

The blood shows the consequence. Triglycerides are markedly higher and HDL is lower, the same lipid pattern seen in metabolic syndrome. This happens without any difference in belly fat or in the inflammatory and fat-tissue hormones often blamed for insulin resistance.

This makes a point that's easy to miss. A person doesn't need to be overweight for insulin resistance to start changing where carbohydrate ends up, and a lean body can hide a liver that's busy making fat. It also shows that fat tissue isn't always the first to struggle, and sometimes muscle goes first.

Muscle insulin sensitivity is also one of the most changeable parts of metabolism. Contracting muscle pulls glucose in through a route that doesn't depend on insulin, and regular training improves insulin's effect in muscle over time.

If someone wants to keep the carbohydrate they eat from becoming liver fat and high triglycerides, it's clear that keeping muscle sensitive to insulin matters, and regular exercise along with fewer refined carbohydrates is the most direct way to do that.

He stopped the weekly injection because the nausea finally won. Two months later, the 61-year-old walked into a hospital convinced parts of his body were missing or dead. 

He was paranoid, hearing and seeing things that weren’t there, and sliding into a rare delusion called Cotard’s—where the mind decides you no longer exist. Doctors later learned he had quit tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) abruptly in August after the side effects became unbearable. He already carried a history of depression, liver disease, and kidney trouble. The timing was hard to ignore. 

Across town that same October, a 52-year-old who had dropped 100 pounds in six months on the same drug simply stopped. Within weeks he was hyperverbal, grandiose, impulsive, and irritable enough that doctors diagnosed a full manic episode and sent him to a psychiatric facility. 

Cannabis use had risen. His B12 was low. He too had a prior anxiety diagnosis. Again, the calendar lined up with the sudden exit from the medication. 

These are two case reports from The Primary Care Companion for CNS Disorders, not a large trial. The authors are careful: they do not claim the GLP-1 caused the psychosis or mania. They note that abrupt discontinuation “may contribute” in certain at-risk people, especially those with nutritional shortfalls or earlier psychiatric history. 

GLP-1 receptors sit in the brain; the drugs can cross the blood-brain barrier. What happens when that signal is suddenly removed is still poorly mapped. Earlier European data had already logged hundreds of psychiatric reports linked to these agents—rare relative to total prescriptions, but not zero. 

The pattern keeps repeating in the literature: some people experience mood or psychotic shifts while on the drugs, others after they come off. Weight returns quickly for most. Muscle can leave with the fat. Hunger and metabolic signals rebound. For a subset, the brain appears to join the list of systems that notice the absence.

The cases are a reminder that these medications rewrite multiple physiological set points at once. Stopping them cold can unmask whatever was being held in check—or simply expose the fact that the underlying drivers of appetite, inflammation, and mood were never fixed. Two hospitalizations do not equal a public-health crisis. 

They do suggest that “just stop when you want” may be more complicated than the marketing implies, and that the people most likely to be prescribed these drugs often already carry the very risk factors that make psychiatric decompensation more plausible.

Three annoyingly reasonable hot takes on the seed oil debate. 🌶️

🌶️ MILD : The debate is almost useless until we define what we're debating.

Hyper-industrialized oils are not the same as omega-6-rich whole foods.

🌶️🌶️ MEDIUM: People over-index on the omega-6:omega-3 ratio.

It's a deceptive metric.

Yes, a lower omega-6:omega-3 ratio is associated with better cardiovascular outcomes and lower mortality.

But higher levels of omega-6 and omega-3 individually, measured in blood and even adipose tissue, are also associated with better outcomes.

TL;DR: the denominator drivers (omega-3)

Most people aren't getting enough omega-3. So rather than obsessing over driving omega-6 toward zero, focus on improving your omega-3 status. I'd pay much more attention to your omega-3 index, aiming for above 8%.

🌶️🌶️🌶️HOT: Claiming that the balance of evidence unequivocally supports seed oils as heart-healthy requires some serious mental gymnastics.

Consider the Minnesota Coronary Experiment.

It's frequently dismissed with speculation about trans fats and concerns over participant dropout. But those objections don't erase the clear bigger picture:

Researchers designed a diet to lower cholesterol by replacing saturated fats with more unsaturated fats.

Cholesterol fell. Death rose. 

Does that prove lowering cholesterol caused death? No.

But that's precisely the point. When we become so fixated on a single nutrient (e.g. saturated fat, or omega-6) we lose of the bigger picture.

hits.text:
3 months on a vegan diet and they lost 5 years worth of muscle! 

Imagine 72 healthy, independent-living adults over 65 who had been eating normally their whole lives. Researchers at Wageningen and Maastricht randomly assigned them to one of three paths for 12 weeks: keep eating the way they always had (omnivorous), switch to a fully self-selected vegan diet, or switch to that same vegan diet while doing supervised resistance training twice a week. 

They weren’t handed rigid meal plans. They got guidance, recipes, and some products, but they chose their own food—the way people actually do in real life. Protein intake in the vegan groups promptly fell from about 1.0 g per kg of body weight down to roughly 0.7 g/kg. Essential amino acids dropped with it. 

MRI scans told the rest of the story. The self-selected vegan group lost about 0.61 liters of thigh muscle volume—roughly 5% of their muscle in just three months. That’s roughly the amount of muscle most people over 50 lose across five ordinary years. Appendicular lean mass fell by more than a kilogram. Muscle protein synthesis rates, measured with deuterium oxide over the first 10 days, were also lower. 

The omnivorous group stayed essentially flat. 

Adding resistance training twice a week helped, but it didn’t fully protect them. That group still lost about 0.35 liters of thigh muscle. The lead author later said she was shocked—she hadn’t expected the exercise group to lose any muscle at all. 

There were other changes. Visceral fat and liver fat dropped in the vegan groups, and body weight fell by a couple of kilograms. Energy intake didn’t clearly crash; the researchers noted the diets simply weren’t matched for protein or energy the way a controlled feeding trial would be.

This sits in interesting contrast to earlier work from the same team. When older adults were given carefully planned, higher-protein vegan meals (around 1.3 g/kg) in a controlled setting for 10 days, their muscle protein synthesis matched the omnivorous diet. Real-world self-selection, especially in people with the anabolic resistance of aging, appears to be a different story. 

The paper’s own conclusion is straightforward: a self-selected vegan diet reduced protein intake, skeletal muscle mass, and muscle protein synthesis in these older adults. Resistance exercise attenuated the loss but did not erase it.

In three months, one dietary shift produced muscle loss that normally takes years. That’s the finding that stands out.

Statins didn't protect the brain.

For years, people have been told a statin might also lower their risk of dementia. That idea came mostly from studies that simply compared people who happened to take statins with people who didn't, and those comparisons are easy to fool.

This week, researchers from Harvard and the VA checked it a much more careful way. They used the health records of men 60 and older who had no heart disease, no diabetes and no dementia, and set the comparison up the way a clinical trial would be: 81,599 men who started a statin versus 843,615 who didn't, followed for 10 years.

After 10 years, 9.4% of the statin group had been diagnosed with dementia, compared with 9.6% of the men who never started one. The authors' own conclusion is that statins don't meaningfully change the risk of dementia.

It's still an observational study, and it was all men. It didn't show the statin hurt the brain, either. It just didn't protect it.

So if you were told a statin would help protect your memory, that promise didn't hold up here. If you're healthy and your doctor wants to start you on one, ask exactly what it's supposed to prevent for you, and by how much.
